questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Leading coefficient and width of a parabola
questions.learningObjective: decide how the leading coefficient changes the width of a parabola
questions.stem: Two parabolas are drawn, one with rule y = x^2 and one with rule y = 4x^2. Which statement describes how the two graphs differ?

options.text: The second is the first moved 4 units downward, because 4 is being subtracted
options.misconception: confuses a multiplier on x^2 with a shift added outside the bracket

options.text: The second is the first reflected across the line y = x, since the exponent changed
options.misconception: believes a change of coefficient swaps the axes of a graph

options.text: The second is narrower, so it reaches a given height at a smaller value of x
The second is wider, so it reaches a given height at a larger value of x
options.misconception: reads a larger coefficient on x^2 as making the graph spread out

questions.explanation: A multiplier on x^2 scales the output, not the input. Fixing a height h, the graph y = x^2 reaches it when x = sqrt(h), while y = 4x^2 reaches it when x = sqrt(h/4), which is half as large. At height 4 the first graph is at x = 2 and the second at x = 1, and the same halving holds at every height, so a larger coefficient on x^2 makes the parabola narrower.
questions.hint: Fix a height, then ask which x reaches it sooner on the wider graph.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Direction of opening and existence of an extreme value
questions.learningObjective: link the sign of the leading coefficient to the extreme value a parabola has
questions.stem: A parabola is given by y = -3x^2 + 5x + 2. Which statement about its graph is correct?

options.text: It opens downward, so it has a least value and no greatest value
options.misconception: confuses the direction of opening with the existence of a minimum

options.text: It opens upward, so it has both a greatest and a least value
options.misconception: ignores the negative sign on the leading coefficient

options.text: It opens upward, so it has a greatest value and no least value
options.misconception: reverses both the direction of opening and which extreme exists

options.text: It opens downward, so it has a greatest value and no least value

questions.explanation: The leading coefficient here is -3, and a negative leading coefficient means the parabola turns over, so the graph falls without limit in both directions and has a single highest point. That point sits at x = -b over 2a, which is 5 over 6, and the height there is 49 over 12. No least value exists, because a downward parabola has no bottom point to read off.
questions.hint: Decide where the parabola turns over before thinking about extremes.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Axis of symmetry read from vertex form
questions.learningObjective: read the axis of symmetry straight off a rule in vertex form
questions.stem: What is the axis of symmetry of the graph of y = (x - 4)^2 + 1?

options.misconception: reads the bracket as a height when it is an input
reads the outside constant as a vertical line of symmetry
swaps the constant and the number inside the bracket

questions.explanation: In the vertex form y = a(x - h)^2 + k, the number h inside the bracket gives the horizontal position of the axis, and k gives the height of the vertex. Here h is 4 and k is 1, so the axis is the vertical line x = 4. The check is that the rule takes equal values at inputs equidistant from 4: at x = 0 and at x = 8 it gives 17 in both cases.
questions.hint: The number inside the bracket gives an input, not an output.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Effect of an outside constant on a graph
questions.learningObjective: describe the vertical shift produced by a constant added outside the bracket
questions.stem: How does the graph of y = x^2 - 7 differ from the graph of y = x^2?

options.text: It is the same graph stretched to 7 times its height
options.misconception: treats a constant outside the bracket as a multiplier

options.text: It is the same graph reflected across the x-axis
options.misconception: reads a change of constant as a change of sign of the whole rule

options.text: It is the same graph moved 7 units down
It is the same graph moved 7 units up
options.misconception: adds the constant instead of subtracting it

questions.explanation: The only difference between the two rules is the -7 added after the square, so every output is reduced by exactly 7 while the input is unchanged. At x = 3 the first rule gives 9 and the second gives 2, and the gap stays 7 at every input, which is the signature of a vertical shift. A change inside the bracket would move the graph sideways, and a multiplier on the square would change its width.
questions.hint: Compare the two rules at the same input and look at the gap.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Non-negativity of a square and the lowest point
questions.learningObjective: use the non-negativity of a square to locate the lowest point of a parabola
questions.stem: For every real number x, the expression (x - 2)^2 is at least 0. What does that tell you about the graph of y = (x - 2)^2 - 5?

options.text: Its lowest point has height -5 and the graph never falls below it
Its lowest point has height 2 and the graph never falls below it
options.misconception: takes the number inside the bracket for the lowest height

options.text: Its lowest point has height -5 and the graph never rises above it
options.misconception: knows the minimum value but attaches it to the wrong extreme

options.text: Its lowest point has height 5 and the graph never falls below it
options.misconception: drops the sign in front of the 5 when reading the vertex

questions.explanation: A square is never negative, and (x - 2)^2 takes the value 0 exactly at x = 2, so the smallest value the whole rule can take is 0 - 5 = -5. That happens at x = 2, which is therefore the vertex. The leading coefficient of a(x - 2)^2 with a positive a is positive, so the graph opens upward and -5 is a floor, not a ceiling.
questions.hint: Ask what the smallest value of the squared part can be, and where.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Counting real solutions from the discriminant
questions.learningObjective: count the real solutions of a quadratic from the sign of its discriminant
questions.stem: A quadratic written as x^2 - 7x + 12 equals 0. How many real solutions does the equation have?

options.text: One, because the discriminant is 0
options.misconception: misreads a positive discriminant as zero

options.text: None, because the discriminant is negative
options.misconception: misreads a positive discriminant as negative

options.text: Two, because the discriminant is 1
Three, because a quadratic always has three roots
options.misconception: counts the two roots plus the vertex as a third solution

questions.explanation: The discriminant is b squared minus 4ac, which here is 49 minus 48, equal to 1. A positive discriminant means the parabola crosses the x-axis twice, so there are two real solutions. Factoring confirms the count, since x^2 - 7x + 12 expands from (x - 3)(x - 4), and the solutions 3 and 4 are indeed two.
questions.hint: Compute b squared minus 4ac before deciding anything about the graph.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Repeated root from a zero discriminant
questions.learningObjective: describe the graph of a quadratic whose discriminant is 0
questions.stem: A parabola is given by y = x^2 - 6x + 9. What does its graph do at the x-axis?

options.text: It cuts the x-axis at two separate points
options.misconception: assumes every parabola crosses the axis twice

options.text: It touches the x-axis at exactly one point, x = 3
It misses the x-axis completely, staying above it
options.misconception: confuses a zero discriminant with a negative one

options.text: It lies along the x-axis for the whole range of x
options.misconception: reads a single contact point as an entire coincident graph

questions.explanation: The discriminant is 36 minus 36, so it is 0, and the rule is the perfect square (x - 3)^2. A square is 0 only at its own centre, so the graph comes down to the axis, touches it at x = 3, and rises again without ever passing through. The quadratic formula confirms a single repeated solution, since it collapses to -b over 2a, which is 6 over 2, that is 3.
questions.hint: A repeated solution comes from a perfect square in the rule.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Negative discriminant and the x-axis
questions.learningObjective: state the condition that keeps a parabola off the x-axis
questions.stem: Which condition on the coefficients a, b and c guarantees that the graph of y = ax^2 + bx + c never meets the x-axis?

options.text: The discriminant is zero
options.misconception: thinks a repeated root means the axis is never reached

options.text: The discriminant is positive
options.misconception: believes two crossings count as missing the axis

options.text: The leading coefficient is negative
options.misconception: uses the direction of opening rather than the number of crossings

options.text: The discriminant is negative

questions.explanation: The discriminant tells you how many times the graph meets the axis, because it is the quantity under the square root in the quadratic formula. If it is negative there is no real value of that square root, so the parabola has no zeros at all. For 2x^2 + 3x + 5 the discriminant is 9 minus 40, which is -31, and the rule stays positive everywhere.
questions.hint: Ask how many real square roots the discriminant permits.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Axis as the midpoint of two roots
questions.learningObjective: locate the axis of symmetry as the midpoint of the two roots
questions.stem: A parabola crosses the x-axis at x = -2 and at x = 6. Where does its axis of symmetry lie?

options.misconception: negates the midpoint of the two roots
subtracts the smaller root from the larger without halving
adds the two roots instead of halving the sum

questions.explanation: A parabola is mirror-symmetric, and its two roots are mirror images in the axis, so the axis must sit halfway between them. Here the halfway point of -2 and 6 is 2. Testing on a rule with those roots, 2(x + 2)(x - 6) takes the value 24 at x = 1 and at x = 3, which are the two points equally far from x = 2 on either side.
questions.hint: The two roots are mirror images across the axis, so halve their sum.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Horizontal distance between two x-intercepts
questions.learningObjective: compute the distance between the two x-intercepts of a parabola
questions.stem: A parabola has its x-intercepts at x = 1 and at x = 8. What is the horizontal distance between those two intercepts?

options.misconception: adds the two intercepts rather than subtracting them
reads off the larger intercept without using the smaller one
multiplies the two intercepts instead of subtracting

questions.explanation: Distance along the number line is the larger value minus the smaller, so the gap is 8 - 1 = 7 units. The sum of 9 is the position of the axis of symmetry, not a distance, and the product of 16 is what a rule with leading coefficient 1 would have as its constant term, so both of those numbers come from the wrong operation.
questions.hint: Distance along a number line is a subtraction, not a sum or a product.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Vertex coordinates from a rule in vertex form
questions.learningObjective: read both coordinates of the vertex from a rule in vertex form
questions.stem: The graph of y = -2(x - 3)^2 + 10 has a turning point. What are its coordinates?

options.misconception: keeps the input position but drops the sign of the height
swaps the two numbers so the height comes first
reads the bracket as x + 3 and so mirrors the axis

questions.explanation: In vertex form the number inside the bracket is the input coordinate of the vertex and the number outside is its height, so the point is (3, 10). Expanding to standard form gives -2x^2 + 12x - 8, and the rule -b over 2a there is 12 over 4, which is 3, confirming the first coordinate. The negative leading coefficient makes this a highest point, not a lowest one.
questions.hint: Write the rule as a square plus a constant and read off both numbers.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Range of a downward-opening parabola
questions.learningObjective: give the range of a parabola that opens downward
questions.stem: What is the range of the rule y = -(x - 2)^2 + 15?

options.misconception: reads the vertex height as the lowest value instead of the highest
negates the vertex height as well as the direction
negates the vertex height but keeps it as a floor

questions.explanation: The bracket is squared and then multiplied by -1, so the rule is at most 15, with equality at x = 2. Because the parabola opens downward there is no lowest point at all, so the range runs upward to the vertex height without a lower bound. Reading the 15 as a floor would mean the graph opens upward, which the negative sign rules out.
questions.hint: Work out whether the graph turns over or opens out before bounding it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Evaluating a quadratic at a given input
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a rule in vertex form at a stated input
questions.stem: Using the rule y = (x - 2)^2 - 3, what is the value of y when x = 5?

options.misconception: reports the constant that is subtracted
squares the input without subtracting the 2 first
treats the bracket as x + 2 instead of x - 2

questions.explanation: Substituting x = 5 into the bracket gives 5 - 2 = 3, and 3 squared is 9, and 9 - 3 is 6. Expanding the rule first gives x^2 - 4x + 1, and at x = 5 that is 25 - 20 + 1, again 6. Two routes agreeing is the check that the bracket was read with the right sign.
questions.hint: Do the bracket arithmetic before the square.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Recovering the symmetric partner of an input
questions.learningObjective: recover the input symmetric to a given one about the axis of symmetry
questions.stem: The rule y = x^2 - 6x is symmetric about the line x = 3. Which other input gives the same output as x = 2?

options.misconception: uses the other root of the rule rather than the reflected input
multiplies the input by the axis position instead of reflecting it
uses the input itself as the partner instead of its reflection

questions.explanation: The partner of an input lies the same distance the other side of the axis, so it satisfies x_partner = 6 - x, and for x = 2 that is 4. Checking with the rule, the value at 2 is 4 - 12 = -8 and the value at 4 is 16 - 24 = -8, the same. The value at 0 is 0, which is what the other root gives, so it is a coincidence of this rule and not the reflection.
questions.hint: The partner input is the reflection of the given one in the axis.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Average rate of change across an interval
questions.learningObjective: compute an average rate of change for a quadratic over an interval
questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of the rule y = x^2 between x = 1 and x = 4?

options.misconception: divides the change in y by the smaller input value
reads the final input as the rate of change
reports the change in y without dividing by the change in x

questions.explanation: Average rate of change is change in y divided by change in x. The rule rises from 1 at x = 1 to 16 at x = 4, a rise of 15 over a run of 3, and 15 over 3 is 5. The 3 alone is only the length of the interval, and the 15 alone is the total change, so neither is the rate until the division is done.
questions.hint: Rate of change is a change in y divided by a change in x.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Constant first differences and second differences
questions.learningObjective: distinguish linear and quadratic behaviour from a table of differences
questions.stem: A table of values for a function has first differences of 3, 3, 3 and 3. What follows from that?

options.text: The rule is linear and its second differences are all 3
options.misconception: reads the first differences as the second differences

options.text: The rule is linear and its second differences are all 0
The rule is quadratic and its second differences are all 3
options.misconception: confuses the constant first difference with a nonzero second one

options.text: The rule is quadratic and its second differences are all 0
options.misconception: calls a constant first difference evidence of a quadratic

questions.explanation: First differences that never change are the fingerprint of a straight-line rule, so a rule such as 3x produces exactly this table. The second differences are found by subtracting consecutive first differences, and 3 - 3 is 0 at every step. A quadratic would have a constant nonzero second difference instead, so the correct reading is linear with second differences of 0.
questions.hint: Subtract consecutive first differences to see whether they stay put.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Second difference of a quadratic rule
questions.learningObjective: obtain the constant second difference of a quadratic from its coefficients
questions.stem: The rule y = 2x^2 + x - 3 is tabulated at consecutive whole-number inputs. What is the constant second difference of that table?

options.misconception: multiplies the leading coefficient by four instead of two
reports the leading coefficient rather than twice it
reports the size of the linear coefficient

questions.explanation: For a rule with leading coefficient a, the second difference is always 2a, and here a is 2, so the second difference is 4. Building the table confirms it: the values at x = 0 to 4 are -3, 0, 7, 18, 33, whose first differences are 3, 7, 11, 15, and subtracting those in turn gives 4 at every step.

questions.topic: Second difference of a quadratic fitted to three points
questions.learningObjective: find the second difference of a quadratic fitted to three given points
questions.stem: A rule passes through the points (0, 5), (1, 8) and (2, 15). What is the constant second difference of the quadratic that fits those three points?

options.misconception: divides the second difference of the table by two and calls that the answer
reads the constant term of the rule as the second difference
adds the first difference to the second difference of the table

questions.explanation: The three outputs are 5, 8 and 15, so the first differences are 3 and 6, and the single second difference is 3, which is not constant until more points are added. Extending the fitted rule settles it: solving the three conditions gives y = 2x^2 + x + 5, and the values at x = 0 to 4 are 5, 8, 15, 26, 41 with second differences of 4 at every step, matching twice the leading coefficient 2.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Choosing a rule from the direction of opening and the axis
questions.learningObjective: choose a rule from the stated direction of opening and axis of symmetry
questions.stem: A parabola opens upward and its axis of symmetry is the line x = -1. Which rule could be its equation?

options.misconception: gets the axis right but reverses the direction of opening
keeps the axis but flips the sign of the height of the vertex
puts a minus sign in the bracket and so mirrors the axis

questions.explanation: The axis is the number inside the bracket, so x = -1 needs a bracket of (x + 1), and opening upward needs a positive multiplier. Only y = (x + 1)^2 - 4 satisfies both. Checking it directly, the rule is stationary at x = -1 and its leading coefficient is positive, so the vertex at (-1, -4) is a lowest point.
questions.hint: The bracket fixes the axis; the sign in front of the square fixes the direction.

questions.topic: Reading a greatest height from a quadratic model
questions.learningObjective: read a greatest height and the time it occurs from a quadratic model
questions.stem: A ball's height in metres after t seconds is modelled by h = -5t^2 + 20t. Which statement about the model is true?

options.text: The greatest height is 20 metres, reached at t = 4 seconds
options.misconception: doubles the time when solving for the vertex

options.text: The greatest height is 5 metres, reached at t = 2 seconds
options.misconception: reads the leading coefficient as the height

options.text: The greatest height is 10 metres, reached at t = 2 seconds
options.misconception: halves the vertex height instead of evaluating the rule

options.text: The greatest height is 20 metres, reached at t = 2 seconds

Substituting gives -20 + 40 = 20 metres. Writing the rule as -5(t - 2)^2 + 20 makes the same vertex visible, since the -5 square term is never positive.

questions.topic: Vertex input of a rule in standard form
questions.learningObjective: find the input coordinate of the vertex from a rule in standard form
questions.stem: The rule y = x^2 - 8x + 3 describes a parabola. What is the x-coordinate of the vertex? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The input coordinate of the vertex is -b over 2a, which is 8 over 2, so 4. Completing the square confirms it independently: x^2 - 8x + 3 becomes (x - 4)^2 - 13, since (x - 4)^2 expands to x^2 - 8x + 16 and the constant must drop by 13 to return 3. The vertex is therefore (4, -13).

questions.topic: Greatest value of a rule written with a square

questions.topic: Positive solution of a difference of squares

questions.topic: Sole solution of an equation built from a square
questions.learningObjective: solve an equation in which a squared factor equals zero
questions.stem: How many solutions does the equation (3x + 6)^2 = 0 have, and what is that single solution? Report the solution.
questions.explanation: A square is 0 only when what it holds is 0, so 3x + 6 = 0 and x = -2. There is no second solution, because squaring has hidden the sign but the left side can never be negative. Expanding to 9x^2 + 36x + 36 and applying the quadratic formula returns the repeated value -2, and substituting gives 3(-2) + 6 = 0 whose square is 0.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Constant after completing the square
questions.learningObjective: find the constant produced by completing the square
questions.stem: Complete the square for the rule y = x^2 + 6x + 5, writing it as y = (x + h)^2 + k. What is the value of k? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Half the linear coefficient 6 is 3, and squaring that gives 9, so the bracket becomes (x + 3)^2. The original constant 5 is smaller than 9 by 4, so k is -4. Expanding to check, (x + 3)^2 - 4 gives x^2 + 6x + 9 - 4, which is x^2 + 6x + 5, exactly the rule given.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Window during which a model stays above a level

questions.stem: A thrown ball follows h = -4t^2 + 16t + 28 in metres. For how many seconds is its height above 40 metres? Report the number of seconds only.
questions.explanation: Setting the height to 40 gives -4t^2 + 16t + 28 = 40, which factors as -4(t - 1)(t - 3), so the model is at 40 metres at t = 1 and again at t = 3, and the parabola opens downward, so it is above 40 metres between those times, a window of 2 seconds. A second route confirms it: the vertex is at t = 2 with a height of 44, so the model drops 4 metres from the peak in a time of 2 divided by 4 under the coefficient, which is 1 second each side of t = 2, again 2 seconds in total.

questions.explanation: Setting the model equal to 32 gives -2t^2 + 12t + 16 = 32, or -2t^2 + 12t - 16 = 0, and dividing by -2 gives t^2 - 6t + 8 = 0, which factors as (t - 2)(t - 4). Both roots solve the original equation, since the height is 32 at t = 2 and again at t = 4, and the earlier is 2. The two times appear because a downward parabola rises through a height and later falls back through it.
questions.hint: Solve for the time, then keep the earlier of the two roots.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Next table value from a constant second difference

questions.stem: A table for a function has value 4 at x = 0 and value 9 at x = 1, and its second differences are constantly 6. What is the value at x = 2? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The first difference from 4 to 9 is 5, and a second difference of 6 means the next first difference is 5 + 6 = 11, so the value at x = 2 is 9 + 11 = 20. A second route gives the same figure: a second difference of 6 means a leading coefficient of 3, and the three conditions 4 at 0, 9 at 1 and value v at 2 give the rule 3x^2 + 2x + 4, whose value at 2 is 12 + 4 + 4 = 20.
questions.hint: A second difference adds to the first difference, it does not replace it.

Expanding first gives x^2 - 3x - 10, and the constant term -10 is the y-intercept, agreeing. The intercept is below the axis, and the roots -2 and 5 both sit to the right of it, so the rule is negative there, as expected.

The vertex is the lowest point of the whole parabola, so nothing inside the interval can beat it.

options.text: 7 and 11
6 and 13

keeps the vertex input but flips the sign of the vertex height
puts a plus sign in the bracket and so moves the vertex to x = -2

reports the constant term of the expanded rule as the height
reports the later root as though it were the height

questions.topic: Building a rule from given zeros

questions.stem: A rule in standard form is known to have zeros exactly at x = -1 and at x = 5. Which rule could be it?

turns the sign of the second bracket round and loses the zero 5
puts the sign of the first zero inside the wrong bracket

questions.explanation: A bracket x minus r is zero exactly at x = r, so the zero -1 needs x + 1 and the zero 5 needs x - 5. Multiplying gives y = (x + 1)(x - 5), and substituting each zero confirms it: at x = -1 the first bracket is 0, and at x = 5 the second is 0. options.text: x <= 3 or x >= 3
options.misconception: uses the sign of the constant instead of its square root
confuses the radicand with the input that gives it

questions.explanation: A square root of a real number needs its radicand to be non-negative, so x^2 - 9 must be at least 0, which happens when the absolute value of x is at least 3. doubles the leading coefficient, so x = 1 gives 10 not 9
adds a linear term the table never shows, so x = 1 gives 14

has the right axis but its lowest value is -8, not -9

Read the number inside the bracket as the input coordinate
Evaluate the rule at that input to get the height
Check the pair against a short table of values

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why a vertex carries an extreme value
questions.learningObjective: explain why the vertex of a parabola is an extreme point of its rule
questions.stem: Explain why the vertex of a parabola gives an extreme value of its rule, and say how you can tell whether it is a greatest or a least value.

answer.exemplar: Every rule of the form y = ax^2 + bx + c can be written as y = a(x - h)^2 + k for some numbers a, h and k, and the rewriting is an identity, so it changes nothing about the values the rule takes. A square is never negative, so (x - h)^2 has a smallest possible value of 0 and takes it at x = h. Multiplying by a turns the picture over: if a is positive the square term is smallest exactly where the whole rule is smallest, so the vertex (h, k) is a lowest point and the rule is at least k for every input; if a is negative the square term is largest where it is zero, so the vertex is a highest point and the rule is at most k for every input. The sign of a therefore decides which of the two extreme values the vertex carries, and that sign is visible directly in the rule, whether it is written in standard form or in vertex form. The reason can also be seen from the vertex formula -b over 2a, which is exactly the input at which the rate of change of the rule is zero, that is, the input at which the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the reverse.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for a reason and a test, and the reason is the non-negativity of a square once the rule is written as a square plus a constant. The test is the sign of the leading coefficient, which is the same number that appears in front of the square, so no expansion is needed to apply it. The example h = -2(t - 6)^2 + 48 shows the test at work, since the negative multiplier makes 48 a ceiling rather than a floor.
questions.hint: Rewrite the rule as a square plus a constant, then reason about the square.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Non-negativity of a square and a lowest point
questions.learningObjective: explain why a square is non-negative and what that fixes about a vertex
questions.stem: Explain why a squared quantity can never be negative, and use that fact to describe the lowest point of the graph of y = (x - 3)^2 - 10.

answer.exemplar: A square is non-negative for every real input because the two factors that make it, x - 3 and x - 3, are always the same sign, so their product can never be opposite-signed and can only be 0 or positive. Equality happens exactly when the factor is 0, that is at x = 3, so the smallest value the square term takes is 0 and no smaller value is available at any input. In the rule y = (x - 3)^2 - 10 the square term is then shifted down by 10, which changes every value by exactly 10 and so makes the smallest value -10 rather than 0, still reached at x = 3. The leading coefficient is positive here, so the graph opens upward and (3, -10) is a lowest point, with the graph never dipping below height -10. Notice that the 3 and the 10 play different roles: the 3 fixes where the lowest point sits horizontally and the 10 fixes how low it is.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for a general reason and then an application, and the general reason is that a square is a product of two equal-signed factors, which can only be 0 or positive. Applying it to the given rule means the square term bottoms out at 0 at x = 3, so subtracting 10 makes the lowest point -10. The explanation also has to say which extreme it is, and the positive leading coefficient settles that.
questions.hint: The two factors in a square are always the same sign as each other.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: How second differences reveal a quadratic rule
questions.learningObjective: explain why constant second differences identify a quadratic rule and fix its leading coefficient
questions.stem: A table of values for a rule has constant second differences. Explain what that tells you about the rule, and show why the constant is twice the leading coefficient.

answer.exemplar: Taking first differences of a table removes the constant term of a rule, because a constant contributes equally to every value and so cancels in a difference. Taking second differences removes the linear term as well, which is why a constant second difference signals a rule of degree two. To see the value of the constant, consider the rule y = ax^2 + bx + c tabulated at the consecutive inputs n, n + 1 and n + 2. The first differences are a(2n + 1) + b and a(2n + 3) + b, whose difference is 2a regardless of n, b or c. The leading coefficient has therefore dropped out and only 2a survives, which is why the second difference is a constant and why that constant is twice the leading coefficient. Recovering the rule from the table means halving the second difference to get a, then using one table value to fix b and c. Worked through: a table with values 4, 9 at the first two inputs and a second difference of 6 gives a leading coefficient of 3, the linear coefficient 2, the constant 4, and the next value 20.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for a mechanism and a proof, and the mechanism is that each round of differencing drops the degree of a rule by one. The proof is the three-value calculation, in which everything except a cancels and leaves exactly 2a. The worked case also shows the practical payoff, since halving the second difference is the quickest route to a leading coefficient and hence to the whole rule.
questions.hint: Take differences of a rule of degree two and watch the degree drop.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Why a quadratic model crosses one height twice
questions.learningObjective: explain why a downward quadratic model can reach one height at two times
questions.stem: A height model h = -2t^2 + 12t + 16 is said to reach 32 metres twice. Explain why a quadratic model can pass through the same height twice, and find the two times.

answer.exemplar: A downward-opening parabola rises to a single highest point and falls away on both sides, so any height below that peak is met once on the way up and once on the way down. That is a property of the shape, not a quirk of this rule, and it is why a quadratic model is not one-to-one: the same output can come from two different inputs. Setting h equal to 32 gives -2t^2 + 12t + 16 = 32, and collecting terms gives -2t^2 + 12t - 16 = 0, which after dividing by -2 is t^2 - 6t + 8 = 0. Factoring as (t - 2)(t - 4) shows the two roots are t = 2 and t = 4 seconds, and the quadratic formula returns the same pair. Both check: at t = 2 the height is -8 + 24 + 16 = 32, and at t = 4 it is -32 + 48 + 16 = 32. The peak of the model is 34 metres at t = 3, so 32 lies just below it, which is exactly the condition for two crossings rather than none.

questions.explanation: The stem asks for an explanation and the actual times, and the explanation is the shape of a downward parabola together with the fact that it is not one-to-one. The computation is set up by making the two sides equal, and the context check matters because a later crossing is often the one wanted. Comparing the target with the peak, which is 34 metres here, confirms that two crossings are possible at all.
questions.hint: Compare the target height with the peak of the model first.
